primary_claim: In a toy MLP trained to compute Boolean logic gates with full enumeration and known ground truth, observational faithfulness (matching input-output behavior, even under noise and out-of-distribution transformations) is not sufficient to distinguish which of multiple candidate subcircuits is the 'correct' explanation of the full model's computation.

effect.metric: subcircuit-vs-full-model output/logit agreement under noise and OOD transforms
effect.value: multiple subcircuits achieve perfect bit-level accuracy and remain indistinguishable even under noise perturbation and out-of-distribution multiplicative transforms; rankings between subcircuits are inconsistent across tests and reverse depending on training regime (with vs without noise)

contradicts_or_qualifies: Replicates the finding by Meloux et al. that many incomparable subcircuits achieve perfect accuracy on a toy task
stated_future_work: Investigate under what conditions full-model fidelity to the ground truth constrains the distinguishability of its subcircuits
Investigate the relationship between full-model fidelity and the smallest domain neighborhood needed for observational tests to be informative
Next post in the series: break open the black box and test whether interventions can succeed where observation could not
limitations_stated: This is a toy setting with full enumeration and known ground truth; results are suggestive, not conclusive
In real models the alignment between the full model and the generator is much less perfect than in the toy models
quote: We cannot definitively differentiate the two subcircuits based on observations, even when evaluating on out-of-distribution inputs. It seems that just looking at inputs and outputs is not enough.
